justification: No factual error found. run-code is green four separate runs in a row (blocks=24, executed=12, exit 0 every time, including the two stack-overflow-crash blocks), so the writer's claim of no flakiness holds. I independently re-derived the article's central and most sophisticated claim rather than trusting it: wrote my own from-scratch program (different method name, different shape — a tail-recursive product accumulator, not the article's sum accumulator) that reflects on its own compiled DLL with System.Reflection.Metadata/PortableExecutable, dumped the full 21-byte IL stream as hex, and manually decoded it instruction-by-instruction (ldarg/ldc.i4.1/conv.i8/ble.s/sub/mul/call token 0x06000003/br.s/ret). The recursive call is a bare `call` (0x28) immediately preceded by `mul` (0x5A); there is no 0xFE byte anywhere in the stream, so `FE 14` (tail.) is genuinely absent — this is airtight, not just a passing boolean from re-running the writer's own scanner. I also independently reran the 3-way behavioral test with my own renamed programs (RunningTotal/RunningTotalTail): non-tail/Debug crashed at 19,295 frames, tail-form/Debug at 19,294 (essentially identical, as claimed), tail-form/Release at 32,127 (higher, as claimed, but still a crash, not a loop) — and reran the article's exact Overflow.cs verbatim, which crashed at 19,282 frames with 'caught it' never printing, matching 'somewhere around 19,000' and the uncatchable claim precisely. Confirmed the try/catch demo genuinely proves the catch never fires: tools/run-code.mjs compares the block's combined stdout+stderr against the article's exact `text output` block (no 'caught it' line present, verified in tools/run-code.mjs lines 230-232); if the catch had ever fired, run-code would fail, so the negative claim is enforced by the harness itself, not merely asserted. Fetched all four cited primary sources directly and checked the exact language: StackOverflowException docs literally say 'You can't catch a StackOverflowException object with a try/catch block, and the corresponding process is terminated by default' (article's paraphrase is accurate); Thread(ThreadStart, Int32) docs literally say 'the default stack size (1 megabyte)' and 'If a thread has memory problems, the most likely cause is programming error, such as infinite recursion' (both quoted correctly, and the article correctly scopes the 1 MB claim to what this specific constructor overload's docs say rather than over-generalizing to all threads everywhere); OpCodes.Tailcall docs give the table entry 'FE 14 | tail. | Subsequent call terminates current methods' and the sentence 'the current method's stack frame should be removed before the call instruction is executed' verbatim; the dotnet/runtime Tail call JIT conditions doc confirms 'we tail call whenever we're allowed to' for the 64-bit JIT and the disqualifying-conditions list (synchronized methods, value-type parameter layouts, address-of-local via ldloca, etc.) the article summarizes. Traced the DirectorySize demo by hand: 120+540+310+275+2048=3293, matching both the recursive and iterative outputs; the four directories (root, src, tests, assets) match the 'directories visited: 4' claim. Traced the permutations find-the-bug exercise by hand for letters=[A,B,C] with the second Swap deleted and got exactly ABC, ACB, CAB, CBA, ABC, ACB — matching the article's claimed buggy output and its 'BAC and BCA never appear, ABC/ACB repeat' analysis exactly. Traced the naive-Fibonacci call tree by hand (C(n)=C(n-1)+C(n-2)+1, C(4)=9 total calls) and the per-n tallies (fib(0)=2, fib(1)=3, fib(2)=2, fib(3)=1, fib(4)=1) both match the program's real output and the SVG figure's node count and highlighted-subtree structure exactly. Checked the .NET version claim: `dotnet --version` on this machine is 10.0.401, matching the article's stated toolchain. Checked the scope boundary: grepped the whole article for Big-O/complexity notation and found none outside the single sentence that explicitly defers Fibonacci's growth analysis to the planned `complexity/analyzing-loops-and-recursion` companion article, which is correctly filed in docs/crosslinks/algorithms/recursion.md (not linked directly, per the brief's rule for unpublished siblings) — the article stays genuinely non-quantitative about recursion's cost, as it claims to. Verified against CONTENT_PLAN.md's own row for this article (§7.3, algorithms #3): title, shape (W), outline order, diagrams and code all match what was actually written, exactly. Against the field: GeeksforGeeks's C# recursion page (fetched directly) has no mention of tail calls, IL inspection, or whether StackOverflowException can be caught at all — confirms the common shallow-tutorial pattern the brief warns about. Wikipedia's Tail call article, which surveys tail-call support language by language (Scheme, Erlang, F#, Kotlin, Rust, Swift, etc.), omits C#/CIL entirely — even the general reference source most likely to cover this has nothing on the exact question this article settles by direct measurement. This is a genuinely differentiated, rigorously self-verified treatment: it does not repeat the common wrong claim that C# has guaranteed TCO, and unlike vague 'it's complicated' hedges elsewhere, it opens the compiled assembly and counts bytes, then backs that up with an independently reproducible empirical crash test across three build configurations. Technical substance here is a clear step above binary-search's round-1 9-ish substance score, and this article does not repeat that article's citation mistake — all four front-matter sources are cited exactly once each, inline, at the sentence they support.
